title: Formation of the New Testament
summary: The New Testament is the second half of the Christian Bible, compiled from the 2nd century. Early 2nd-century writings show knowledge of the four gospels and of collections of Paul's letters. Marcion, who died around 160, is an early figure in the forming of canons. The earliest surviving list of the same 27 books in today's Bible is the Easter letter of Bishop Athanasius of Alexandria in 367.

uncertainty.note: Early collections of gospels and Pauline epistles were recognized by the early 2nd century; the 27-book canon was fixed by Athanasius in 367 CE and confirmed at the Council of Carthage in 397 CE.

as_recorded.value: Muratorian Fragment, dated anywhere from 170-200 to the 4th century CE

where.modern_name: Mediterranean; stand-in pin at Alexandria, Egypt
where.historical_name: Alexandria, Diocese of the East, Roman Empire

importance.justification: Defined the canonical 27-book Christian New Testament, creating the central textual foundation of Western religion, ethics, and culture.

related.because: The life, teachings, and crucifixion of Jesus and early apostolic ministry produced the underlying oral traditions and texts that formed the New Testament.
